content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors attempt to deconstruct three widely held ideas on mutual information in contrastive learning. 

Specifically, the paper claims that i) batch size in contrastive learning need not be small, ii) in contrastive learning mutual information is relevant to the downstream task performance, and iii) task-irrelevant information isn't detrimental to the generalization of the downstream task in contrastive learning.

Additionally, the author propose an alternative of data augmentation consisting of drawing positive pairs by sampling them from the same class. This has the advantage that the mutual information being maximized is known in closed form. 

The superior empirical results obtained by the authors lead them to question whether contrastive learning should really be thought of as an unsupervised method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**- Strength:** 

The idea that, so long as the class information $c$ can be recovered perfectly from features $x$ and $y$, the mutual information $I(y; x)$ is known in closed-form, is simple yet novel and interesting.

**- Weaknesses:**

**I am not sure 'Correction 2' is sound.** What makes MI relevant or not for the downstream task isn't MI itself, but how the positive pairs are constructed.  The choice of augmentation/sampling of positive pairs ensures that the learned representations do not factor in how one element of the pair is specific relative to the other. 

By choosing the label as the class to sample positive pairs from, the authors are effectively ensuring features capture all between-labels specificities and ignore within-label specificities. This is precisely what a vanilla classifier would do implicitly. 

It is therefore unclear what benefits mutual information estimation in the proposed method brings over straight up classification.

**I am not sure 'Correction 3' is sound either.** As I mentioned earlier, features are learned in a manner that ensures that the corresponding representations are consistent in both elements of a positive pair. Adding transformations that have nothing to do with the downstream task will result in feature vectors that contain more information than necessary to solve the downstream task.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper reads well, the contribution is novel, and results seem reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper reads well but the three corrections aren't strong enough, and questionable for some.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
Overall, this paper attempts to take a closer look at the role and behavior of mutual information as an objective or target as used in representation learning.

In particular, the paper attempts to correct three beliefs: (1) That small batch size hurts InfoNCE training, (2) that MI doesn't correlate well with downstream performance and (3) that optimal representation learning ought to target *minimally* relevant representations.

The paper also invites a broader discussion about whether we should view constrastive representation learning methods are truly unsupervised at all.

The paper discusses each in turn and uses illustrative experiments to demonstrate their findings.  The appendix includes details and additional experimental results and discussion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
To its strength, the paper takes a deeper look at some subtle issues in representation learning and in particular information theoretically motivated contrastive representation learning.

 Overall, I like papers like this. I like papers that try to take a closer look at some fundamental assumptions researchers make and make use of carefully designed setups to help disambiguate them.  I certainly agree that a good number of papers and researchers hold incorrect views about mutual information and contrastive learning and that papers in this mold can really help to clarify things.  Unfortunately, and probably one of the hardest things for me to get over is that I feel as though *this* paper also commits similar sins.

The paper discusses contrastive representation learning as if the goal is to learn representations that have high mutual information, but with, I fear, the unstated assumption that this is somehow a difficult thing to do.  But we know it isn't.  If you want to learn representations that contain the maximum amount of information with respect to any possible downstream task you wish, the answer is simple: simply do nothing!  If you're representation $h$ was the identity map, you could preserve all of the information.  It doesn't have to be the identity, any invertible function would preserve all of the information, including exotic ones like some kind of cryptographically secure random permutation or embedding of the original image into lower dimensions.  It's not difficult to form representations with lots of information.  We should expect that essentially any randomly initialized neural network representation will preserve essentially all of the information contained in their inputs (since the outputs are distinct for all inputs you test).

If we merely wanted to ensure we had representations with high mutual information with all possible downstream tasks, the answer is clear, do nothing to the input.  In fact, we can say something stronger.  By data processing inequality we know that if we do anything non-invertible, its not as if the situation can ever improve, it can only possibly get worse.  So why then do we engage in this business at all?  It has to be due to reasons beyond mutual information.  It has to be because maybe we aren't just interested in a representation that preserves information, we want a representation that preserves the information and has nice statistical or geometric properties. Maybe it can be resolved with something like a linear or two layer probe (where-as we know that the original image cannot).  Maybe its lower dimensional, or satisfies other constraints we might care about.  This is a much more nuanced discussion, but I fear this paper doesn't quite get there. 

As a quick aside: I don't think its such a modest assumption to assume that you can perfectly classify, but that's a nit more than anything.

## First Belief
Consider the first belief.  The paper claims that it is a widely held belief that contrastive learning requires large batch sizes because of InfoNCE's O(log K) bound.  I think they are correct in saying that that is a commonly held belief.  The paper instead claims that the batch size limits the training loss but neither the information learned nor the downstream-task performance.  It illustrates this by using their CDP dataset, and the class matched augmentation.  This is nice because in this setup we have a good sense of what the true mutual information should be.  They train multiple representations at different batch sizes and report the training loss, as well as an independent estimate of the mutual information (using a reinitialized discriminator and a larger batch size).

Strengths: This experiment does, very clearly, show that the training batch size doesn't explicitly limit the mutual information between the learned representations or the downstream task performance. 

 Unfortunately, I feel as though this kind of misses the mark.  As we discussed above, if we instead understood that essentially any neural network representation will preserve essentially all of the information, we wouldn't find these results surprising.  Perhaps this is a sign that there is a deeper misunderstanding to focus on?  As a concrete suggestion, I suggest the authors repeat their analysis but attempt to lower bound the mutual information between the images themselves $I(X,Y)$ for which they should also find ~6 bits, as well as for a randomly initialized encoder, for which, I strongly suspect they will also find ~6 bits if they do a "post-training" evaluation but without any actual training.

That being said, I feel as though these experiments also might miss the mark in the sense that the take away is that we should not worry about the batch size when it comes to learning our representations, but honestly if anything there is a hint in the results that we might have cause to worry.  For the smallest batch size of 2, there is a noticeable gap that opens up between the post-training MI and the expected 6 bits. Granted, 6 > 2 as the paper is want to point out, but 6 isn't that much greater than 2 if we are being honest.  This might be relevant because for a lot of the kinds of augmentations that people use in contrastive learning, we should expect that the mutual information between two views of the same image is >> 6 bits.  Its certainly as high as a few dozen and potentially as high as a few thousand bits (depending on the strengths of the augmentations).  If that's the case, we might worry that there could be a more substantial effect of training with low batch size, more akin to what appears to be starting to show up here at a batch size of 2.

How do I reconcile what I just said with what I said in the previous paragraph?  Well, even though I expect that even a randomly initialized network will have a lot of mutual information between its representations, I'm not necessarily sure that the two layer MLP critic used here will have the easiest time seeing that.  I could see it either being the case that the smallest batch size experiment here either didn't put enough pressure on the learned representations to be distinguishable by the small critic, or alternatively, it might be the case that while the InfoNCE doesn't explicitly *compress* the learned representation, the effective of training might act to.  This feels like a deeper and more important question to explore.  The first step to distinguishing between these two possibilities would be to measure the mutual information in the original images as well as for the randomly initialized encodings.

## Second Belief
The second belief the paper investigated was that: the mutual information cannot measure how effective the representation is for downstream tasks.  The paper instead contends that the only metric strongly relevant to the downstream-task is the MI of the downstream-talk information itself.

First, I feel though the paper is a bit unfair to Tschannen et al. 2019 here. I don't feel as though that paper was trying to say that MI *cannot* measure how effective the representation is, instead they showed an explicit example of where higher measured MI meant lower downstream performance.  To steelman Tschannen et al, I don't think the point was that MI *can't* indicate downstream performance but that in some cases it doesn't.  And they weren't wrong in that.

So, to investigate this claim the paper computes a whole set of proposed metrics for downstream performance and evaluates their correlation with downstream classification.  They discover that yes, the $I_{\text{SimCLR}}$ information doesn't correlate all that well with downstream classification while the $I_{\text{class}}$ does, and is the best predictor of downstream performance.

Here again, to its credit, the paper does make a convincing demonstration of their claim.  However, here again, to its weakness I feel as though the paper sort of misses the point again.

One thing I was expecting to see mentioned in the work, is that we could interpret the likelihood of any non-linear classifier as itself a lower bound on the mutual information (using $C$ for *class*):
$$ I(X;C) = \mathbb{E}_{p(x,c)} \left[ \log \frac{p(c|x)}{p(c)} \right]  \leq \mathbb{E}\_{p(x,c)}\left[ \log \frac{q(c|x)}{p(c)} \right] = \mathbb{E}\_{p(x,c)}[ \log q(c|x) ] + H_p(C) $$
(which is (10-12) in the paper but with the variables changed.)
This let's us interpret the performance of any downstream classifier's likelihood $q(c|x)$ as a variational lower bound on the mutual information as well, assuming we either know, or can bound the entropy of the label distribution.  This could have been used, for instance in the these experiments in addition to, or instead of the Accuracy column as another direct probe of the amount of label information retained in the learned representation, i.e. it could estimate $I(h_X; C)$

In light of this, Section 3.2 is a bit silly.  The overall result is that if you use a contrastive lower bound to estimate $I_{\text{class}}(h_X,h_Y)$ you discover that it correlates very well with downstream classification accuracy.  However, we know that the downstream classifier likelihood is itself a lower bound on: $I(h_X; C)$  We also know by data processing that $I(h_X; h_Y) \leq I(h_X; C)$ and expect that it should nearly saturate this bound.  So, the result of Section 3.2 is that two different attempts to measure the same quantity are better correlated than attempts to measure other things.  In this light the results don't seem all that surprising.  The only thing I feel as though this is really measuring is the correlation between downstream classifier likelihood and classifier accuracy, which we already expect should correlate strongly.

As an aside and concrete ask: I would like to have seen a scatterplot representing Table 2, of $I_{\text{class}}$ versus Acc, and $I_{\text{SimCLR}}$ versus Acc.  I trust my eye more than I trust either Kendall or Pearson.

## Belief 3

The third belief the paper investigated was that: To design optimal views, task-irrelevant information needs to be discarded for better generalization.
Instead the paper claims "Task-irrelevant information do not necessarily harm the generalization of the downstream task."

In this case I take some explicit issue with the wording of the correction. It should be modified to, minimally: "Training contrastive losses for additional task-irrelevant information does not necessarily harm the generalization of the downstream task."  

The issue is that the experiments can't say whether or not the learned representations in the lesser cases (color, digit, position) don't themselves contain information about the other attributes.  The results in Figure 5 appear to be a *linear* probe of the downstream accuracy.  The likelihood of a linear probe could be interpreted as a lower bound of the mutual information, but its also only a linear probe.  How can we be sure that the representation learned when trained using only the "color" objective doesn't itself contain all of the information about "digit" and "position"?  Not because of some magic but just because the learned representation might contain essentially *all* of the information contained in the original image (provided its practically invertible).  We don't actually know whether the "Color" representation contains less information than the "All" representation, we know only that the "All" representation has a representation that makes the "digit" information, say, linearly resolveable.  It could be the the "color" representation also has that information but requires something beyond a linear probe to extract.

The paper's experiments and the results in Figure 5 do demonstrate clearly that training for the "All" case doesn't hurt downstream linear performance on any of "color", "digit" or "position" and as the paper points out, at least in a couple cases it does slightly better.  Though, I'm not convinced its truly better, for that I'd need to see more than a single run and that it consistently does better. (A concrete TODO to consider).

To really address the *spirit* of the question here, the paper would have had to attempt to measure or explicitly *compress* the learned representations.  The real question is whether, if we train a whole family of representations with different amounts of mutual information, whether those that were smaller while otherwise retaining the useful information generalized better than the more expressive representations.  For example, if the paper had learned compressed representations using a tractable *stochastic* encoder and a variational *upper* bound like those discussed in the referenced Poole et al. 2019 it could have trained a 1-bit, 2-bit, 4-bit, 6-bit, 12-bit and 100-bit say representation of the images targeting "Color" and see whether there were systematic differences in the generalization of the over-parameterized representations as compared to the 2-bit, potentially minimally-sufficient one.  But that wasn't done here.

"When a specific positive pairing is used for training, we would expect only the corresponding information to be learned in the representation." - This direct quote I think highlights the unease I felt reading the paper where as I discussed at the start, where it seems to highlight the false belief that it is somehow difficult to learn representations that retain downstream information.  Rather, I believe, its nearly the opposite.  By pushing up on a lower bound of mutual information, there is nothing keeping the mutual information *low*.  There is no pressure in the objective itself to *limit* the amount of information in the learned representation.  In so much as training does limit information that has to be due to some implicit regularization in the optimizer or initialization of the network.

## Discussion Section

The discussion section opens by saying that since the paper observed that $I_{\text{class}}$ was an effective metric of downstream performance, we might expect it to work well for training.
As we discussed above, $I_{\text{class}}$ is basically a direct way of measuring downstream classifier likelihood.  A downstream classifier likelihood is directly a lower bound on $I(h_X;C) \geq I(h_X; h_Y)$.  In Table 12, I would have liked to see a straight up classification baseline and classification baseline with the same data augmentation scheme used in the self-supervised schemes.

The next section questions whether we should really think of "unsupervised" learning methods as truly unsupervised.  It makes the valid, and I agree underappreciated point that the choice of augmentation itself is a guidance signal for learning, and that overall the effectiveness will be determined by the overlap between the augmentation information and the downstream target information.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I had trouble judging how to separate out my review between the previous and this section.

In terms of clarity, the paper is well written and clear in its exposition.  My biggest issue is the sorta meta-clarity issue where-in I feel as though the paper misses the mark in the sense that I feel as though while the paper does make a correct step in the right direction with regards to the three misconceptions it discusses, there is a sort of deeper misconception the paper misses and doesn't address, in that it isn't difficult to retain downstream information as I tried to elaborate above.

In terms of quality, I believe the paper does a good job illustrating the points it was trying to make with the experiments it did and the way it presented the results.

In terms of originality, I believe the experiments presented here are all new, though aspects of the issues talked about here have appeared in other work, but not in a way that I think renders this work unoriginal in a meaningful way.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I have a bit of difficulty with this one.  I like the goal the paper is working towards and feel as though for the most part the claims made in the paper are correct and well demonstrated.  At the same time, I can't help but feel as though the paper misses the mark at a higher level, sort of missing the forest for the trees.

This means that while I don't technically disagree with most of the content of the paper, I sort of spiritually disagree.  Maybe one way to say it is that I feel as though the paper generally gives correct answers to what I feel as though are the wrong questions.

That being said, I feel as though this paper is a positive contribution to the community and does a good job seeding useful conversations, and so currently I am learning towards accept.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This submission attempts to invalidate the three common beliefs regarding contrastive learning below. It reaches the following conclusions:
Although a small batch size limits the maximum value of the train-time InfoNCE estimator, it does not limit the maximum amount of mutual information (MI) between views that the representation can contain. As shown empirically, when training with a small batch size, the post-training InfoNCE MI estimated between examples belonging to the same class can be much higher than the maximum value of the InfoNCE bound during training.
Mutual information is a better measure of representational quality than other measures proposed in previous work, including uniformity, alignment, tolerance, and linear CKA. When measuring correlations between measures of representational quality and downstream accuracy across many networks, the InfoNCE MI lower bound correlates better than these other metrics.
Augmentations do not necessarily have to be designed to eliminate all task-irrelevant information. Contrastive learning can be effective even when information is shared between views.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
There are a large number of misunderstandings regarding information theory and contrastive learning, and attempting to correct these misunderstandings is a worthy goal.
The paper is clearly written and experiments are clearly described. The red and green boxes make it easy to understand the claims that are being refuted.
Statements made are generally well-supported by experiments.

Weaknesses:
Contrary to what is claimed, I believe that belief 2 is actually correct. The paper’s argument is empirical in nature and relies on replacing MI with the InfoNCE estimator. However, the InfoNCE estimator can be an arbitrarily poor estimator of MI.
The counterexamples are empirical and, especially for beliefs 2 and 3, provide little insight into why the original beliefs are wrong.

More detailed notes:

Belief 1:
I agree that this is a common belief among people who do contrastive representation learning, and with the paper’s “correction.”
It would be a good idea to double-check that this claim is actually made by the cited work. For example, I think the results of McAllester and Stratos relate to dataset size, not minibatch size.
In practice, people use InfoNCE when L2-normalized representations, and doing so prevents the loss from ever saturating, since the contrastive probability distribution cannot achieve zero entropy.

Belief 2:
The discussion of this point conflates mutual information with the InfoNCE lower bound. The InfoNCE bound can be a poor measurement of the true amount of mutual information but still reflect the quality of the representation for downstream tasks, which was among the points made by Tschannen et al. (2019). Mutual information is invariant under homeomorphisms, but homeomorphisms can reduce both the InfoNCE bound and the accuracy of a linear classifier to zero. The idea that the InfoNCE estimator (or any distribution-free estimator) accurately measures MI is a harmful existing belief in itself, and I do not believe it should be perpetuated.
It seems somewhat trivial to me that the InfoNCE estimator of MI between images belonging to the same class will be better-correlated with accuracy than alternative estimators considered, especially given that computing the value of this estimator requires the same knowledge of the downstream task labels as training the linear classifier. Effectively, it measures whether an image is closer to another image belonging to the same class than to images belonging to different classes, whereas alignment and uniformity don’t use the labels, tolerance does not contrast distances in the same class to distances between classes, and linear CKA is strange to use in this context for reasons described below. I suspect that it should also be possible to lower bound the MI estimated here from the cross entropy of the linear classifier itself.
In the context of neural network representations, linear CKA is usually used to compare representations across different networks or different layers of the same network. Measuring linear CKA between representations of two views from the same layer of the same network seems a bit strange, since CKA is supposed to deal with orthogonal transformations between representation spaces, but if the representations come from the same network then they reside in the same space. I’m not aware of previous work that has used the approach that the authors apply here. 
The representation evaluation metrics that involve two views can all be applied either to two augmentations or two images of the same class. In fact, if the feature extractor produces normalized output, then alignment and tolerance are effectively equivalent (since $\|f(x) - f(y)\|^2 = 2 - 2 f(x)^\top f(y)$). Thus it would make sense to consider each with and without label information utilized.
Kendall/Spearman correlation may be better than Pearson correlation for the kinds of analyses in Table 2. This is clear for the CDP models where the supervised and self-supervised models have very different accuracies and simply differentiating between these groups is sufficient to explain most of the variance.


Belief 3:
I’m a bit torn on what to make of this belief. On one hand, I agree with the authors that there are situations where “task-irrelevant information do not necessarily harm the generalization of the downstream task” (at least to a meaningful degree) including those shown here. On the other hand, there are obvious cases where task-irrelevant information *does* harm generalization on the downstream task, such as the experiments in Tian et al. (2020b) and feature suppression examples of Chen et al. (2021a).
The CDP dataset seems at least superficially similar to the Colorful-Moving-MNIST dataset from Tian et al. (2020b), but there, varying all factors is clearly suboptimal. What accounts for the discrepancy?

Discussion:
In Section 4.1, it is claimed that optimizing a lower bound on $\hat{I}_\text{class}$ may not be optimal for representation learning. I don’t find this very surprising. The situation seems analogous to ERM where minimizing the empirical risk is not necessarily the best way to minimize the true risk and regularization can improve results. It also appears that $\mathcal{L}_\text{class}$ always matches or exceeds the authors’ SimCLR results; the numbers from other papers may not be directly comparable due to differences in experimental setup or the budget used for hyperparameter tuning.
The statement “While a high performing network must have its representation express the downstream-task information very well as we have shown in Section 3.2” seems frustratingly hand-wavy to me. Is there any more specific way of phrasing this?
Section 4.2 may be extrapolating a bit too far from the sample of metrics considered in Section 3.2 when suggesting that “the only metric that is truly effective for predicting downstream task’s performance is the downstream-task information itself.” For example, Reed et al. (2021) show that linear rotation prediction accuracy can be a good proxy for accuracy on the downstream task. 

References (only those not in paper):

Reed, C. J., Metzger, S., Srinivas, A., Darrell, T., & Keutzer, K. (2021). Selfaugment: Automatic augmentation policies for self-supervised learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 2674-2683).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is clear.

Quality: The experimental setup seems reasonable. However, many statements in the paper are factually imprecise or incorrect. See my detailed notes above.

Novelty: Aspects of this work exist in previous work, but, if the other issues described were resolved, I could potentially be persuaded that the results have value. Off the top of my head, the following previous results seem similar to those provided here:
Although it is certainly common lore that contrastive learning needs large batch sizes, Appendix B of Chen et al. (2020a) provided results with batch sizes 256 to 8192 showing smaller batch sizes have only a minor impact on accuracy, and this impact can potentially be recovered through longer training. The experiments here are somewhat complementary, since they show insensitivity to batch size on synthetic data in terms of MI rather than on real data in terms of linear eval accuracy.
As noted above, the experiments related to belief 3 are at least superficially similar to those that Tian et al. (2020b) conduct with the Colorful-Moving-MNIST dataset.

Reproducibility: The provided details seem sufficient to reproduce the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper makes an attempt to clarify the information theoretic basis for contrastive learning. The topic is important and the writing is generally clear. However, several of its statements seem either imprecise or incorrect, particularly those involving belief 2.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper challenges the three basic beliefs regarding to Mutual Information (and its empirical realization InfoNCE loss) in contrastive learning: 1) small batchsize leads to worse bound of Mutual Information (MI), 2) many metrics (except for MI) in contrastive learning can be useful for measuring downstream tasks (without downstream labels), and 3) task-irrelevant information needs to be discarded to achieve better generalization in the downstream tasks. The paper mostly shows empirical evidences on a synthetic datasets (CDP), where a specific data augmentation technique is used (same-class augmentation) and the exact value of mutual information can be computed and manipulated. Some theoretical results are also shown.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The paper challenges some common knowledge ground in contrastive learning and can trigger insightful discussion. 
2. The paper has interesting experiments to demonstrate their stands. 

Weakness
1. Some theoretical argument is simply wrong. 

For example, in Eqn. 16. Why $\mathcal{L}$ is always nonnegative? Note that the denominator which has $2K - 1$ terms, doesn't include the nominator term, and thus the ratio can be greater than 1, when $f(x_i)$ and $f(y_i)$ have high similarity. So the proof in A.3 doesn't seem to be correct. While the paper claims that *"It is a well-known fact that the estimated MI in Eq. (2) is upper bounded by $\log (2K_{Tr} − 1)$"*, I didn't really find this acknowledgement from any of the four references listed by the authors (Oord
et al., 2018; Sordoni et al., 2021; McAllester and Stratos, 2020; Poole et al., 2019). 

2. There are over-claims. 

For example, in Sec. 3.2, the paper claims that *"The only metric that is strongly relevant to the downstream-task performance is the MI of the downstream-task information itself."*. While the paper shows that a few existing metrics (e.g., Alignment, Uniformity, etc) do not correlate well with the the performance of the downstream tasks, saying *any* metric other than downstream MI is not strongly relevant is an overkill. There exist other metrics in contrastive learning.

3. The connections among the three basic belief points are weak. 

From the paper, it seems that the three points are disconnected. Do they have any relationship? Why the authors put them together in the same paper? It would be great if the authors show their relationships, otherwise the readers only get rather limited signals. 

4. Others
In Eqn. 1. What is $l(i,j)$? $j$ has already been summed over in the denominator of the equation? Is that just $l(i)$?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is readable, but there is still room for improvement. The abstract and intro can be done better: currently there is no clear conclusions after reading abstract/intro. While these beliefs are wrong, what are the correct ones? 

Also I didn't understand the logic chain from the failure of common beliefs (if these are really not true) to the follow-up questions on whether contrastive learning is unsupervised. Can the authors explain a bit further? This point seems to be really disconnected from the main point of the paper, but appears in both abstract/intro. 

In terms of novelty, the paper seems to raise good questions on existing common beliefs. 

Reproducibility: the paper seems to be easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the paper is interesting but still requires a lot of works to meet the bar of top-tier conference like ICLR.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper takes a critical look at established beliefs about the mechanics underlying modern contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) and their connection to mutual information maximization. Specifically, the paper re-examines the relevance of large batch size in the context of contrastive SSL, the effectiveness of mutual information to predict downstream performance, and the relevance of careful view design for downstream performance. In summary, the paper arrives at the roughly opposite conclusions compared to previous work w.r.t. these three aspects.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I agree with the general narrative of the paper, that despite a large body of literature on the topic, there are still many aspects of contrastive SSL that are not fully understood. In that regard, I think the paper’s angle has high relevance for the SSL community.

However, I feel 1) that the paper represents some claims it addresses from the prior literature in a somewhat inaccurate manner, and 2) that most of the arguments the paper brings forward are not very convincing. In more detail:
- While I see the usefulness of constructions like $\hat I_\text{class}$ in the context of theoretical work as a tool to construct proofs, where the quantity is likely not relevant for the final result, I believe it makes less sense for a mainly empirical paper as the present one. - As for the first aspect of contrastive learning addressed by the paper, namely the issues with small batch size: Sure, it seems that for $\hat I_\text{class}$ on the synthetic data set constructed by the authors a small batch size does not hurt performance, but will this generalize to non-synthetic data sets and losses that are not using class information but are relying on per-instance augmentation? The paper does not answer this question, so it does neither correct nor confirm the existing believe, which is based on different data and view construction.
- Similarly, for belief 2: The insight that MI is not a good predictor for downstream performance is purely based on the *MI estimated on upstream data* without using class labels of the downstream task. Of course if one includes labels of the downstream target task, one can construct better predictors for the downstream task, arguably the best ones are the accuracy/metrics measured on a downstream testing set, and unsurprisingly $\hat I_\text{class}$ correlates with those. But again, the paper completely changes the setup compared to prior work, so its correction is not valid.
- As for belief 3: While the experiment is interesting, I think the picture might change as the data set becomes more complex and the capacity of the model smaller compared to the data set complexity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly well written and easy to follow. The practical evaluations seem well done overall, covering multiple models and metrics to make the analysis robust. A lot of additional detail is provided in the appendix.

However, as stated above under “Strengths and weaknesses” I doubt the relevance of the insights.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses the relevant topic of better understanding contrastive SSL and re-examining existing beliefs. The arguments brought forward do not seem very convincing to me.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Correcting Three Existing Beliefs on Mutual Information in Contrastive Learning

content.title: Thanks for your review!
content.comment:
Dear reviewers,

Thank you very much for your thorough review and clear feedback. As all of the reviewers have agreed, indeed we believe there are many aspects of MI and SSL that need to be understood better.  In particular, we have encountered numerous arguments are conclusions that are not sufficiently rigorous and our goal was to develop rigorous methods and point out how some of the existing beliefs can be misleading. 

After reading your reviews, however, we also agree that our own statements are not rigorous enough. Therefore, we will withdraw our work and make proper corrections according to your feedback. 

Again, we truly appreciate your careful review.
